title: Set up your computer
summary: Install a code editor, run your first page in the browser, and learn the loop you will repeat for every lesson in every course. Do this once and you are ready for everything else.
objectives: Install VS Code and the extensions this course assumes
Create a project folder and open it in the editor
Run an HTML page in a real browser and see your changes immediately
Know the edit, save, refresh loop you will repeat for every lesson

blocks.text: You need two things to write code: an editor to type it in, and a browser to see the result. Everything on this site is free, and so is every tool below.

rows: The editor. It highlights your code, catches typos and runs tasks.
To open your pages. Chrome, Firefox, Edge or Safari all work.
Needed once we reach JavaScript, so install it now.

items: Open code.visualstudio.com/download and download the installer for your operating system.
Run the installer. On Windows, tick "Add to PATH" and "Open with Code" when it asks.
Open VS Code. You should see a Welcome tab. Close it, you do not need it.
Press Ctrl+Shift+X (Cmd+Shift+X on macOS) to open the Extensions panel.

blocks.text: The Extensions panel is where you install everything else. Every extension below is installed the same way: search for its name, click Install, and wait for the button to change.

items: Live Server: opens your page in the browser and refreshes it every time you save. This is the one you will use constantly.
Prettier: formats your code so it stays readable. Set it as your default formatter.
Auto Rename Tag: when you rename an HTML tag, it renames the closing tag for you.
Error Lens: shows mistakes directly on the line instead of hiding them in the problems panel.

blocks.text: Prettier only formats on save if you tell it to. Open Settings with Ctrl+, then search for "format on save" and tick the box. Every time you save a file from now on, your indentation and spacing get tidied automatically.
Make one folder where all your practice lives, for example called code-practice on your Desktop. Do not put it inside another project. Inside it, create a file called index.html.

Open the folder in VS Code with File, then Open Folder, and pick code-practice. The file list appears on the left. This is called a workspace, and you will open it the same way every time you sit down to practise.

blocks.caption: index.html - your first page
blocks.text:
Hello, world

If you can read this in your browser, you are set up.

items: Right-click index.html in the file list and choose "Open with Live Server".
Your browser opens with a local address such as 127.0.0.1:5500. That is your page, served from your own computer.
Go back to VS Code, change the text inside the h1 element, and press Ctrl+S to save.
Look at the browser. The page already changed. You did not press refresh.
This is the loop: edit, save, look. It is the same loop for the rest of your life as a developer.

blocks.text: If the browser shows a file list instead of your page, you right-clicked the folder rather than index.html. Also make sure the file really is named index.html, not index.html.txt - hiding file extensions in your operating system is the usual cause.

rows: Save. Save before you look at the browser, every time.
Comment the selected line out. Useful for testing what happens without a line.
The command palette. If you cannot find a command in a menu, it is here.

blocks.text: How to use this site while you practise

Each lesson has content to read, tasks to try in your editor, and a quiz to check yourself. Do the tasks in the editor, not in your head. Reading code teaches you to recognise it; typing it teaches you to write it.

items: Read the lesson, but keep VS Code open beside the browser.
Type every code example into your file by hand instead of copying it. Typing is how the syntax enters your fingers.
Save and look at the browser after every change.
Do the tasks, then tick them off. Your progress is saved in this browser.
Take the quiz. If you get one wrong, read the explanation, then try the task again.

blocks.text: Nothing you write here can break anything. Your files are on your own computer, and you can always delete the folder and start again. Experiment freely - that is what the folder is for.
A page that looks wrong nearly always has one specific cause. Before asking for help, check these four things in order.

items: Did you save the file? An unsaved change is invisible in the browser and is the single most common mistake.
Is a closing tag missing? Browsers are forgiving but will nest your content inside the wrong element.
Is the file in the right folder? A path like images/photo.png only works if that folder really exists next to your HTML file.
Is the browser showing an old version? Press Ctrl+Shift+R to reload without the cache.

blocks.text: You will spend more time reading error messages and your own code than typing new code. That is not a sign you are bad at this. It is the job.

tasks.prompt: Install VS Code, then install the four extensions from step 2. Confirm each one shows as installed.
tasks.hint: Extensions panel is Ctrl+Shift+X on Windows and Linux, Cmd+Shift+X on macOS.

tasks.prompt: Turn on format on save in the settings, then deliberately mess up the indentation in index.html and press Ctrl+S. Confirm Prettier tidies it.
tasks.hint: Search settings for "format on save" and tick the checkbox. If nothing happens, check that Prettier is your default formatter.

tasks.prompt: Create index.html with the example from step 3, run it with Live Server, and change the heading text while watching the browser update on save.
tasks.hint: Right-click the file itself, not the folder.

tasks.prompt: Break it on purpose: delete the closing </body> tag, save, and note what the browser does. Then put it back.
tasks.hint: Seeing how a browser recovers from broken markup removes the fear of breaking it.

quiz.question: You changed your HTML, saved the file, but the browser shows the old page. What is the most likely cause?
options: The browser cache is always the problem
The file was not actually saved, or Live Server is not running
HTML cannot be changed after the first load
You need to reinstall VS Code
quiz.explanation: An unsaved file, or a Live Server session that is no longer running, explains almost every "my change did nothing" moment. Check the save first, then the server, and only then suspect the cache.

quiz.question: What does Live Server actually do?
options: It uploads your page to the internet
It compiles your HTML into JavaScript
It serves your folder locally and refreshes the browser when you save
quiz.explanation: Live Server starts a small web server on your own machine pointing at your folder, and tells the browser to reload whenever a file changes. Nothing leaves your computer.

quiz.question: Why type the examples by hand instead of copying them?
options: Copying is blocked by the browser
Typing is faster once you are experienced
Typing builds the muscle memory and forces you to notice the syntax
quiz.explanation: Copying gets the result on screen without teaching you anything. Typing makes you read every character, which is where the syntax actually sticks.

quiz.question: Your page ignores the CSS and shows plain text. What should you check first?
options: Whether the file path to the stylesheet in the link tag is correct
Whether the CSS file is over 100 lines
quiz.explanation: Styles, images and scripts are found by path. If the path does not match the file's real location and name, the browser loads nothing and applies nothing.
